title: Ad Click Event Aggregation (Real-time)
problem: Design a real-time ad click event aggregation service that powers advertiser reporting and near-real-time budgeting.
summary: A streaming aggregation pipeline: ad clients fire impression/click beacons into an edge ingest tier, events are queued on Kafka with idempotency keys, Flink maintains per-(ad_id, minute) counters with event-time tumbling windows, and aggregates land in a columnar OLAP store (ClickHouse) for advertiser dashboards. A nightly batch corrector re-aggregates raw events from cold storage (S3) to fix late-arriving clicks and bot-filtered rows — the streaming result is 'fast but approximate', the batch result is 'authoritative'. The dominant design choice is a lambda-style stream + batch reconciliation over a pure streaming system: exactly-once aggregation at the click volume here (1B/day, peak ~50K clicks/sec) is expensive, and advertisers will accept a stream that's eventually corrected overnight. The main tradeoff is dual-path complexity — two codebases must produce the same schema.

functional: Ingest click and impression beacons from millions of browsers and apps with an idempotency key
Produce per-(ad_id, minute) aggregates available to advertisers within about a minute
Support per-campaign and per-advertiser rollups over hour, day, and lifetime windows
Enforce campaign budget caps in near real time by reading the streaming counters
Tolerate out-of-order and late-arriving events up to a bounded watermark
Expose a query API for advertiser dashboards with sub-second latency on recent data
nonFunctional: Sustain 50,000 clicks/sec steady state with headroom for 5x traffic spikes
Streaming aggregates visible within 60 seconds of the originating click
No data loss: every accepted event must appear in either the streaming or batch rollup
Nightly batch correction must reconcile with streaming to within 1% before publishing
Horizontal scale on both ingest and aggregation — no single broker or worker is a bottleneck
Cost per billion events must fall year-on-year as the fleet grows

assumptions: 1B click events/day (100:1 impressions:clicks → 100B impressions/day — not all stored)
Peak 3x sustained for major events (Black Friday, Super Bowl)
Event size ≈ 400 bytes (ad_id, user_id, ts, geo, device, creative_id, publisher)
Advertiser queries: 'impressions & clicks for campaign X last 7 days, grouped by creative'
SLA: streaming aggregates visible within 1 min; batch reconciliation by T+24h
estimates: Daily raw volume: 1B * 400B = 400 GB/day clicks; plus ~40 TB/day impressions
Aggregated rows: ~10M active ads * 1440 minutes = 14.4B cells/day into ClickHouse, but heavily compressible (~95% compression ratio on counters)
Query QPS: advertiser dashboards ≈ 500 concurrent, 2 queries each per load → ~50 QPS on OLAP

architecture.mermaid: graph LR client[Ad Client] --> ingest[Edge Ingest] ingest --> kafka[Click Kafka] kafka --> flink[Stream Aggregator] flink --> olap[(OLAP Store)] flink --> dlq[Dead Letter Queue] s3[Raw Event Lake] --> batch[Batch Corrector] kafka --> s3 batch --> olap olap --> reportapi[Report API] reportapi --> dashboard[Advertiser Dashboard]

client.name: Ad Client (SDK / Pixel)
client.summary: JavaScript pixel or mobile SDK embedded on publisher pages that emits impression and click beacons.

sections.heading: Event shape
Fire-and-forget
sections.body: Clicks are sent as `navigator.sendBeacon(...)` so the page can navigate away immediately. The beacon is best-effort — the network layer handles retries, but a dropped event is acceptable (we'll correct overnight).

sections.heading: Client-side dedupe
sections.body: event_id is a client-generated UUID — identical retries carry the same id so the edge ingest can dedupe without adding round trips.

sections.heading: Clock skew
sections.body: Phone clocks can be minutes off. The edge stamps a trusted `ts_server_ms` on receipt; downstream aggregation keys on that, not on `ts_client_ms`.

bottlenecks.title: sendBeacon drops on page navigation
bottlenecks.trigger: User clicks ad and browser navigates to advertiser URL within milliseconds; at 11.6K clicks/sec sustained (35K/sec peak) even a 1-2% drop rate loses 10-20M clicks/day. Some browsers cap sendBeacon payload at 64KB and silently drop if queue is full or if navigation happens before the beacon is dispatched.
bottlenecks.symptom: Streaming click counts run 1-5% below batch-corrected numbers consistently; advertisers complain numbers 'jump up' after overnight reconciliation; mobile Safari shows worse loss than Chrome.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Fire the beacon on `mousedown`/`touchstart` instead of `click` so it dispatches before navigation; keep payload well under 64KB (strip optional fields); fall back to a synchronous 1x1 pixel GET (`/px?...`) if `sendBeacon` returns false. Tag events with a `dispatch_method` field to measure per-path loss.
bottlenecks.detection: Compare stream vs batch click counts per hour per browser/OS in a dashboard; alert when `(batch - stream) / batch > 2%` for any segment. Also emit a client-side `beacon_queue_full` counter via the next successful beacon.

bottlenecks.title: Client clock skew corrupts event-time windowing
bottlenecks.trigger: Phone clocks drift minutes to hours off real time; `ts_client_ms` from ~1% of devices is off by >2 min (the Flink watermark allowance). At 11.6K clicks/sec that is ~10M skewed events/day routed incorrectly if any downstream uses client time.
bottlenecks.symptom: If any code path (debugging, A/B attribution, funnel joins) trusts `ts_client_ms`, clicks appear in the wrong minute bucket or the wrong day; DLQ fills with 'late' events that were actually on time server-side.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Never key aggregation on `ts_client_ms` — the edge already stamps `ts_server_ms` and Flink windows on it. Enforce this with a schema-registry contract that marks `ts_client_ms` as diagnostic-only. Additionally, have the edge return its server time in response headers so the SDK can compute and report a `clock_skew_ms` field for monitoring.
bottlenecks.detection: Histogram `ts_server_ms - ts_client_ms` at the edge; alert when p99 skew exceeds 5 min or when >2% of events have skew >2 min (indicates a misbehaving SDK build or regional NTP outage).

bottlenecks.title: event_id collisions / non-unique UUIDs on low-entropy devices
bottlenecks.trigger: `crypto.randomUUID` is unavailable on older browsers (pre-2022 Safari, older Android WebView) where SDKs fall back to Math.random-based UUIDs. With 1B events/day, poor-entropy v4 generators produce measurable collisions; the Flink 24h RocksDB dedupe would then drop legitimate distinct clicks.
bottlenecks.symptom: Streaming counts run slightly below batch even after fixing beacon drop; Flink `duplicates_dropped_last_min` metric is elevated for specific UA classes; affected advertisers see systematically lower stream numbers on mobile web.
bottlenecks.mitigation: In the SDK, prefer `crypto.randomUUID` and fall back to `crypto.getRandomValues(new Uint8Array(16))` to build a v4 UUID; never Math.random. Additionally compose event_id as `{user_id_hash}-{ts_client_ms}-{random}` so collisions require matching all three fields, and have Flink's dedupe key on this composite.
bottlenecks.detection: Track duplicate-drop rate per UA class in Flink; alert when any UA class exceeds 0.1% dedupe rate (baseline is retries only, should be near zero). Sample event_ids offline and check cardinality vs row count per day.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Ad Client is here The whole pipeline exists to count **impressions and clicks that happen on other people's websites** — publisher pages, not our own. We don't control those pages' servers, so the only way to observe "this ad was shown" or "this ad was clicked" is to ship a tiny piece of our code that runs inside the publisher's page and phones home. That's the SDK/pixel. It's also the only place that knows the click happened *before* the browser navigates away to the advertiser's landing page, so it has to fire a beacon in that narrow window. ## What happens without it Without a client component, you'd have no observation point at all — the click is a browser event on a third-party page, and by the time the advertiser's server sees the visitor, you've lost the link back to which ad/creative/campaign drove it. Advertisers would see traffic but couldn't attribute it, billing would be impossible, and the entire downstream pipeline (Kafka, Flink, ClickHouse) would have nothing to aggregate. ## One concrete number The design assumes **1B clicks/day ≈ 11.6K/sec sustained, ~35K/sec peak**, plus 100× that in impressions. Every one of those events originates from a client beacon — there is no other source. If the SDK drops even 2% due to `sendBeacon` losing the race against page navigation, that's 20M clicks/day missing from streaming numbers, which is exactly why the client generates an `event_id` for dedupe and why the batch corrector exists as a safety net. ## Trade-off Putting logic in untrusted third-party pages means accepting clock skew, ad-blockers, and best-effort delivery — which is why this design treats streaming numbers as approximate and reconciles overnight.

ingest.name: Edge Ingest Service
ingest.summary: Thin global edge POP that accepts click/impression beacons, server-stamps timestamps, and publishes to Kafka.

sections.heading: Responsibilities
sections.body:
- Accept `POST /beacon` and `GET /px?...` (pixel)
- Stamp `ts_server_ms`, `edge_pop`, `ip_truncated`
- Lightweight validation: reject malformed JSON, unknown ad_id, obvious bot UAs
- Produce to Kafka; return 204 No Content fast

sections.heading: Why at the edge
sections.body: Beacons are small, geographically dispersed, and latency-insensitive for the user — running the receiver in 30 edge POPs shortens the TCP RTT for the client and batches to the central Kafka over long-haul.

sections.heading: Backpressure
sections.body: If Kafka is unreachable, spill to local disk buffer (NVMe, 60 min retention) and keep accepting. Losing a click is worse than running the edge hot.

sections.heading: Bot filtering (coarse)
sections.body: Block known datacenter IP ranges and obvious headless UAs at the edge. Fine-grained bot scoring happens in the batch layer where we can see the full event graph per user.

gained: No ops for the edge tier
lost: Producing into self-hosted Kafka from edge workers is awkward — usually you ship to Kinesis/Pub/Sub first

bottlenecks.title: Impression topic Kafka produce saturates edge-to-core long-haul
bottlenecks.trigger: Impressions run ~1.16M/sec sustained and ~3.5M/sec at 3x peak. Each event is ~400B, so the edge fleet must ship ~460 MB/sec sustained (~1.4 GB/sec peak) into the central Kafka over long-haul links from 30 POPs. A single POP losing its path to the Kafka cluster (BGP flap, cross-region fiber cut) forces that POP onto disk spill within seconds.
bottlenecks.symptom: Edge producers report rising `record-send-rate` lag and `request-latency-avg`; NVMe spill buffer fills (60-min retention exhausted in minutes at 1M/sec per POP); 5xx rate rises as disks fill; downstream Flink sees a sudden catch-up spike when the link restores, pushing watermark lag past the 2-min allowance and diverting traffic to DLQ.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Batch aggressively at the producer (`linger.ms=50`, `batch.size=1MB`, `compression.type=zstd`) to cut wire bytes ~5x; run a regional Kafka tier per geography and MirrorMaker2 to the central cluster so edge POPs only cross short-haul; size NVMe spill for 2h at peak per POP (~360GB) not 60 min; pre-aggregate impressions at the edge into 1-sec (ad_id, pop) counters before producing — impressions don't need per-event fidelity for the streaming path.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on edge `kafka_producer_buffer_available_bytes` < 20% for >30s, `record-error-rate` > 0, or spill-disk usage > 50%. Dashboard long-haul egress bytes/sec per POP vs. provisioned bandwidth; alert at 70% utilization.

bottlenecks.title: Unknown ad_id cache miss storm during campaign launches
bottlenecks.trigger: Validation rejects 'unknown ad_id' using a local cache. When a large advertiser launches thousands of new ads at once (e.g., seasonal campaign flight), the edge sees a surge of ad_ids not yet in cache. At 35K clicks/sec + 1M impressions/sec peak, even a 1% miss rate = ~10K lookups/sec per POP against the ad-metadata service.
bottlenecks.symptom: Spike in 'unknown ad_id' rejections or DLQ writes immediately after a campaign goes live; p99 beacon latency jumps from ~12ms to 100ms+ as validation blocks on upstream lookups; ad-metadata service sees thundering-herd load from 30 POPs simultaneously.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Treat unknown ad_id as soft-accept: produce to Kafka with an `unvalidated=true` flag and let the batch corrector reconcile — never block the beacon path. Push new ad_ids proactively to edge caches via a pub/sub fanout at campaign-create time (seconds, not TTL-driven). Use a bloom filter sized for all active ad_ids (~10M × 10 bits = 12MB per POP) as a fast negative check with periodic refresh.
bottlenecks.detection: Track `unknown_ad_id_rate` per POP; alert when >0.5% for >1 min. Monitor ad-metadata lookup QPS from edge and alert on sudden step-changes correlated with campaign-create events.

bottlenecks.title: NVMe spill buffer overruns during sustained Kafka outage
bottlenecks.trigger: Spec says 60-min NVMe spill when Kafka is unreachable. At 1M impressions/sec per POP × 400B × 3600s = ~1.4TB/hour raw, or ~280GB/hour compressed at 5x. A single-digit-TB NVMe fills in ~2-4h at sustained peak — shorter than realistic cross-region Kafka recovery windows (regional failovers, ISR rebuilds can take 30+ min).
bottlenecks.symptom: Edge disk usage climbs linearly during Kafka outage; once full, ingest starts returning 503 or silently dropping — losing 20M+ clicks/hour across fleet; on-call pages for disk-full while root cause (Kafka) is still being fixed; post-recovery replay of spooled files creates a backlog spike that blows the 2-min Flink watermark.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Size NVMe for realistic worst-case outage (4h at 3x peak ≈ 3-4TB compressed per POP); compress spill files with zstd; rate-limit replay on recovery (`max.in.flight.requests=5`, throttled producer) so catch-up doesn't outrun Flink; fall back to a secondary Kafka cluster in a different region via a circuit-breaker rather than relying solely on local disk; drop impressions before clicks when spill crosses 70%.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on spill directory usage > 40% (warn) and > 70% (page); gauge `kafka_producer_connectivity_state` per POP and alert on any POP >5 min disconnected; track projected time-to-full based on current fill rate and alert when <30 min.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Edge Ingest Service is here For an ad click aggregation system at 1B clicks/day plus 100B impressions/day, the events originate from SDKs running inside *other people's web pages* all over the world. You can't let those SDKs write directly to Kafka — Kafka isn't designed to be exposed to the public internet, brokers can't authenticate millions of untrusted clients, and the TCP round-trip from, say, a phone in Jakarta to a central Kafka cluster in us-east-1 would be hundreds of milliseconds. The edge ingest service is the thin, geographically-distributed front door that terminates the beacon quickly, stamps a *trusted* server-side timestamp (client clocks lie), does cheap validation and bot filtering, and then hands the event to Kafka over warm long-haul connections it keeps open in bulk. ## What happens without it If SDKs talked straight to Kafka: clients in far regions would see 300ms+ beacon latencies, losing clicks to `sendBeacon` racing against page navigation. You'd have no place to stamp `ts_server_ms`, so Flink's event-time windowing would key on skewed phone clocks and clicks would land in the wrong minute buckets. And the first Kafka outage would drop events on the floor — there's no local disk buffer at the client to spill to. ## One concrete number At peak, the edge handles ~1.4 GB/sec of impressions (3.5M/sec × 400B). Batching at the edge with `linger.ms=50` and zstd compression cuts long-haul bytes ~5×, turning that into ~280 MB/sec of actual Kafka traffic — viable over a handful of cross-region links instead of millions of direct broker connections. ## Trade-off You accept running and patching an extra tier in 30 POPs in exchange for latency, durability, and a trustworthy server timestamp.

kafka.name: Click Kafka
kafka.summary: Durable partitioned log of impression + click events feeding all downstream consumers.

sections.heading: Topics
sections.body: `ad_clicks` (11K–35K/sec) and `ad_impressions` (1M+/sec). Separate topics so consumers can scale independently.

sections.heading: Partitioning
sections.body: Key by `ad_id` so Flink's keyBy(ad_id) is co-located with the partition — no cross-node shuffle. 500 partitions on the impressions topic, 200 on clicks.

sections.heading: Retention
sections.body: 7 days on clicks, 2 days on impressions (volume forces shorter). After retention, events are already in S3 (see sink).

sections.heading: Exactly-once
sections.body: Flink + Kafka transactional producer gives exactly-once sink into the OLAP store using two-phase commit tied to Flink checkpoints.

lost: 1 MB/s per shard cap — many shards at impression scale
No in-order guarantee across publishes by default (must opt-in to ordering keys)

bottlenecks.title: Impression topic partition hot-spotting on keyBy(ad_id)
bottlenecks.trigger: The impressions topic runs ~1.16M events/sec sustained and ~3.5M/sec at 3x peak across 500 partitions, keyed by ad_id. A top-100 advertiser's hero ad can drive 5-10% of daily impressions — that single ad_id pins to one partition, producing 50K-300K msg/sec into a single broker leader while the other 499 partitions idle at ~5K/sec. A single Kafka partition tops out around 50-100 MB/sec (~125K-250K msgs/sec at 400B); the hot partition saturates.
bottlenecks.symptom: Producer-side `record-send-rate` stalls for specific ad_ids while others flow freely; broker hosting the hot leader shows 90%+ CPU and disk I/O while peers are at 20%; Flink subtask owning that partition lags by minutes while other subtasks are caught up — watermark stalls globally and windows fail to close on time.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Switch impressions topic to composite key `hash(ad_id, bucket_minute % N)` with N=8-16 sub-shards, and have Flink do a two-stage aggregation (pre-aggregate per sub-shard, then merge by ad_id). Alternatively key by `(ad_id, user_id_hash % 32)` for natural spread. Keep clicks topic keyed by ad_id (volume is 100x lower so hot-spot is tolerable). Raise impressions partition count to 1000+ so even post-split leaders have headroom.
bottlenecks.detection: Monitor per-partition `BytesInPerSec` on brokers; alert when any partition exceeds 3x the topic-median rate for >1 min. Track Flink per-subtask `currentInputWatermark` skew and alert when the max-min gap exceeds 60s.

bottlenecks.title: Impression topic retention storage blow-up
bottlenecks.trigger: Impressions at 1.16M/sec × 400B × 86400s ≈ 40 TB/day raw. With 2-day retention and 3x replication that's 240 TB of broker disk for impressions alone, before accounting for peak-day surges (Black Friday at 3x = 120 TB/day raw, 720 TB replicated over 2 days). A single broker in a reasonably sized cluster (say 30 brokers) carries 24 TB of impressions data — at the edge of single-node NVMe economics.
bottlenecks.symptom: Disk usage climbs toward 80% on impression brokers; log-segment deletion lags behind ingest during peak days; adding brokers triggers multi-hour partition rebalances that further stress the cluster; cost review flags Kafka as the largest line item in the pipeline.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enable `compression.type=zstd` at producers (5x reduction on JSON-ish events → 8 TB/day). Cut impression retention to 12h (Kafka Connect to S3 runs every 5 min, so 12h is ample replay buffer). Use Kafka tiered storage (KIP-405, Confluent/Apache 3.6+) to offload cold segments to S3 after 1h, keeping only hot segments on broker NVMe. Consider pre-aggregating impressions at the edge into 1-sec counters before Kafka — per-event fidelity isn't needed for streaming.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on broker `kafka.log:type=LogSize` > 70% of provisioned disk per broker; alert on `LogCleaner` / retention-delete lag > 15 min; dashboard daily bytes-in vs. forecast and alert on 2x step-changes.

bottlenecks.title: Transactional producer throughput ceiling under exactly-once + 2PC
bottlenecks.trigger: Flink's exactly-once sink uses Kafka transactions tied to 30s checkpoints. Each checkpoint opens/commits a transaction per subtask across 200 click partitions + 500 impression partitions = 700 partition-transaction markers every 30s. At 35K clicks/sec peak plus 3.5M impressions/sec, transaction coordinator throughput and `__transaction_state` writes become a bottleneck; long-running transactions (30s) also hold up LSO (last stable offset), delaying read-committed consumers.
bottlenecks.symptom: Checkpoint duration grows from seconds to tens of seconds; `TransactionCoordinator` logs show elevated `CommitTxn` latency; downstream read-committed consumers see visibility lag equal to the checkpoint interval; occasional `ProducerFencedException` during checkpoint retries causes Flink job restarts.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Shorten checkpoint interval to 10-15s to reduce LSO lag and transaction size (trade-off: more coordinator load, but smaller per-txn batches). Dedicate a beefy 3-node transaction coordinator set with SSD-backed `__transaction_state` partitions. Set `transaction.timeout.ms` to 2x checkpoint interval. Consider downgrading the impressions path to at-least-once (idempotent producer only) since the batch corrector reconciles anyway — reserve exactly-once for clicks where billing demands it.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on Flink `lastCheckpointDuration` p95 > 20s; monitor Kafka `TransactionCoordinator` metrics `CommitTxnTimeMs` p99 > 500ms; track consumer lag between LEO and LSO on read-committed consumers and alert if gap exceeds 2x checkpoint interval.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why Kafka sits between the edge and Flink For an ad click aggregation service at 1B clicks/day plus 100B impressions/day, the edge ingest tier is producing events *much* faster than any single downstream system wants to consume them, and from dozens of POPs scattered around the world. You need a place to park those events durably while Flink (streaming aggregator), Kafka Connect (S3 archival), and anything else built later all read at their own pace. Kafka is that buffer: a partitioned, replicated log that decouples the "fire 1M events/sec into *something*" problem from the "carefully aggregate with exactly-once semantics" problem. Keying by `ad_id` also means Flink's `keyBy(ad_id)` reads only from its assigned partitions — no cross-node shuffle. ## What happens without it If the edge wrote directly to Flink, a Flink deploy or checkpoint stall would immediately back-pressure the edge, filling its 60-minute NVMe spill in minutes at peak and dropping clicks on the floor — advertisers lose billable events. You'd also have no replay: when the nightly batch corrector wants yesterday's raw events, there's nowhere to read them from except S3, which means a Flink bug caught mid-day can't be fixed by rewinding and re-processing. ## The number that forces it Impressions run ~1.16M/sec sustained (100B / 86400s), ~3.5M/sec at 3× peak. At 400 bytes each that's ~1.4 GB/sec of writes. Spreading across 500 partitions = ~7000 msgs/sec/partition, well within a broker's ~125K msgs/sec per-partition ceiling — but only because partitioning exists as a first-class concept. ## Trade-off You accept running a stateful, disk-heavy cluster (and its ops burden) to gain replay, multi-consumer fanout, and isolation between producers and consumers.

flink.name: Stream Aggregator (Flink)
flink.summary: Consumes click events and maintains per-(ad_id, minute) counters using event-time tumbling windows.

sections.heading: Job DAG
sections.body: `Source(Kafka) → Map(dedupe by event_id via RocksDB state, 24h TTL) → KeyBy(ad_id) → TumblingEventTimeWindow(1 min) → Aggregate(count, uniq users via HLL) → Sink(ClickHouse via JDBC + 2PC)`

sections.heading: Watermarks
sections.body: Event-time watermark trails real time by 2 min to tolerate late events. A click stamped at 14:32:50 with a watermark of 14:34:00 still lands in the 14:32 window. Events later than the watermark go to the dead-letter queue and are handled by the batch corrector.

sections.heading: Dedupe via idempotency key
sections.body: RocksDB keyed-state holds `event_id → seen_ts` with 24h TTL. A retried click from the same SDK won't be double-counted in the streaming path.

sections.heading: Flink code
Checkpointing
sections.body: Checkpoint every 30s to S3. On failure, Flink replays from Kafka from the last checkpoint; the 2PC sink to ClickHouse commits only after checkpoint completion → exactly-once aggregates.

gained: Same engine for streaming and batch (unified dataframe)
Easier for data-engineer teams already on Spark
Runs as a library; no separate cluster
lost: Harder to scale state horizontally past a few TB
Sink connectors less mature than Flink's

bottlenecks.title: RocksDB dedupe state blows past memory/disk budget at 24h TTL
bottlenecks.trigger: Dedupe keyed-state holds event_id → seen_ts with 24h TTL for every click AND impression flowing through. At 1B clicks/day + 100B impressions/day = ~101B keys × (16B uuid + 8B ts + RocksDB overhead ~40B) ≈ 6+ TB of state across the cluster. Even if dedupe is clicks-only, 1B × ~64B = 64 GB/day = 64 GB live state per Flink TM shard group, with compaction write amplification 10-30x.
bottlenecks.symptom: Checkpoint sizes grow from GBs to hundreds of GBs; checkpoint duration exceeds the 30s interval and starts backpressuring the source; RocksDB compaction CPU pins at 100% on TM hosts; p99 per-record latency jumps from ms to seconds; eventually TM disks fill and the job fails into a crashloop that can't recover because restoring state from S3 takes longer than the Kafka retention window (7 days clicks / 2 days impressions).
bottlenecks.mitigation: Restrict dedupe to the clicks stream only — impressions accept at-least-once since batch reconciles. Shorten dedupe TTL to 1h (retries happen within seconds, not a day) cutting state ~24x. Use a probabilistic structure (rolling Bloom/Cuckoo filter per hour) for the dedupe check with a small exact overflow table; or offload dedupe to a Kafka compacted topic keyed by event_id. Size TM local NVMe for 3x peak state and enable incremental checkpoints with RocksDB's `state.backend.rocksdb.compaction.level.use-dynamic-size=true`.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `flink_taskmanager_job_task_operator_rocksdb_live_sst_files_size` growth rate > forecast; alert on `lastCheckpointDuration` p95 > 20s or `lastCheckpointSize` > 2x 7-day baseline; monitor TM local disk usage > 60% and RocksDB compaction pending bytes > 10 GB per subtask.

bottlenecks.title: Hot ad_id keys create subtask skew after keyBy(ad_id)
bottlenecks.trigger: Top advertisers' hero ads take 5-10% of daily volume on a single ad_id. At 35K clicks/sec peak (clicks topic keyed by ad_id into 200 partitions + 500 subtask parallelism), the subtask owning that key processes 2-3K/sec while peers handle <100/sec — 20-30x skew. Worse on impressions at 3.5M/sec peak where a hot ad_id can drive 200K+ events/sec to one subtask, exceeding a single TM slot's throughput (~50-100K events/sec with RocksDB state access).
bottlenecks.symptom: Per-subtask watermark divergence — Flink UI shows one subtask's watermark 60s+ behind peers; busyTimeMsPerSecond near 1000 for hot subtasks while others idle; windows globally can't close because the job watermark = min(subtask watermarks), so ClickHouse sink stalls and 2PC transactions time out; checkpoint barriers block behind slow subtask and checkpoints time out at 30s.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Two-stage aggregation: first `keyBy(hash(ad_id, user_id_hash % 32))` to pre-aggregate partials across 32 sub-shards, then `keyBy(ad_id)` to merge — spreads hot keys across 32 subtasks. Alternatively use Flink's `LocalKeyBy` (pre-aggregate before shuffle) so hot keys never cross the network. Raise job parallelism so even skewed subtasks have headroom; pin hot subtasks to dedicated TM slots via slot sharing groups.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on max-min `currentInputWatermark` across subtasks > 30s; alert on any subtask `busyTimeMsPerSecond` > 800 for >2min; dashboard per-subtask `numRecordsInPerSecond` and alert when ratio of p99 to median > 10x.

bottlenecks.title: ClickHouse 2PC sink commits bottleneck window emission at minute boundaries
bottlenecks.trigger: Every minute, ~10M active ads emit one row into the sink — a 10M-row burst consolidated through the 2PC sink coordinated with Flink's 30s checkpoints. ClickHouse JDBC ingest caps around 100-500K rows/sec per node; a 10M-row batch across a handful of shards takes 20-60s, overlapping the next window's emission. Combined with exactly-once 2PC (pre-commit writes a staging part, commit does `ATTACH PART`), each checkpoint carries hundreds of staged parts per shard.
bottlenecks.symptom: Sink backpressure propagates upstream; Flink UI shows `Sink.busy` near 1000; checkpoint duration climbs toward the 30s interval and occasionally exceeds it, triggering checkpoint timeouts and job restarts; ClickHouse `system.parts` row count grows faster than merges can compact, producing `Too many parts` errors (default limit 300 active parts per partition); aggregates for minute N don't become visible until minute N+2 or later, violating the <1 min SLA.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Buffer and batch multiple minute-windows into a single sink commit coordinated with checkpoints (e.g., emit to a pre-sink queue, flush 1 batch/30s = 1 part/checkpoint per shard rather than per window). Use ClickHouse's native TCP protocol client (not JDBC) for 3-5x ingest throughput. Pre-shard the emit by cityHash64(campaign_id) in Flink so each subtask talks to exactly one ClickHouse shard, avoiding fanout. Raise `parts_to_throw_insert` to 600 and tune `background_pool_size` for faster merges.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on Flink `Sink__ClickHouse.numRecordsOutPerSecond` dropping while input rate holds steady; monitor ClickHouse `system.parts` count per partition and alert at >200; alert on `lastCheckpointDuration` p95 > 25s; track end-to-end latency (event ts_server_ms → ClickHouse visible) and alert p99 > 90s.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why Flink sits between Kafka and ClickHouse For an ad aggregation service promising "streaming aggregates visible within 1 minute," someone has to turn the raw firehose of clicks in Kafka into the per-(ad_id, minute) counters that advertiser dashboards actually query. Flink is doing three jobs that Kafka alone can't: **grouping events by event-time windows** (so a click stamped 14:32:50 lands in the 14:32 bucket even if it arrives at 14:33:30), **deduplicating by `event_id`** (SDK retries and network layers will resend the same click), and **committing exactly-once into ClickHouse** via two-phase commit tied to its checkpoints — so a Flink crash mid-window doesn't double-count or lose a minute's clicks. ## What happens without it If you tried to write raw Kafka events straight into ClickHouse, you'd insert ~11.6K rows/sec of per-event data and then force every advertiser query to do a massive `GROUP BY ad_id, minute` over billions of rows — seconds becomes minutes. Worse, retried beacons would double-count clicks (inflating bills), and late events arriving out of order would silently fall into the wrong time bucket with no watermark logic to catch them. ## One concrete number The design expects ~10M active ads × 1440 minutes = **14.4B aggregate cells/day** landing in ClickHouse. At 1B raw clicks/day, that's a ~70× reduction Flink performs *before* the OLAP store sees anything — turning 11.6K events/sec into roughly 170K pre-aggregated rows/minute, which ClickHouse can ingest comfortably. ## Trade-off You accept running a stateful streaming cluster (RocksDB state, checkpoints, careful tuning) to get sub-minute freshness with exactly-once semantics — the batch corrector exists precisely because even this is only "fast but approximate."

olap.name: OLAP Store (ClickHouse)
olap.summary: Columnar OLAP database holding per-(ad_id, minute) aggregates for sub-second advertiser queries.

sections.heading: Schema
Why ReplacingMergeTree
sections.body: When the batch corrector writes the 'batch' version of a row it replaces the 'stream' version on merge. Advertisers querying with `FINAL` or `argMax(source)` always see the best-available number.

sections.heading: Query pattern
sections.body: `SELECT campaign_id, toStartOfDay(bucket_ts), sum(clicks) FROM ad_agg_1m WHERE campaign_id =? AND bucket_ts >= now - INTERVAL 7 DAY GROUP BY 1,2` — hits one partition per day, seconds-range latency even on billions of rows.

sections.heading: Sharding
sections.body: Sharded by `cityHash64(campaign_id)`, replicated 3x. Each shard holds ~5 days hot; old partitions drop to S3 via `TTL... TO VOLUME 's3'`.

lost: More moving parts than ClickHouse (broker, historical, middle-manager…)

gained: Integrates with AWS data lake tools
lost: Streaming ingest requires Firehose + COPY batches (minutes of lag)
Query latency > ClickHouse at similar cost

gained: Trivial INCR writes; sub-ms reads of a single cell
lost: No ad-hoc OLAP (no GROUP BY across millions of keys)
Hard to backfill corrections without a sweep job

bottlenecks.title: ReplacingMergeTree merge backlog + FINAL query cost during/after batch overwrite
bottlenecks.trigger: Nightly batch corrector writes ~14.4M rows/day for the prior day's partition, duplicating every (campaign_id, ad_id, bucket_ts) key that streaming already wrote. Until background merges complete, each partition holds 2x rows and correctness depends on `FINAL` or `argMax(source)` at query time. At ~10M active ads × 1440 min = 14.4B cells over a 5-day hot window, post-batch merges must rewrite hundreds of GB of compressed parts while the Flink sink is still producing ~170K rows/min into the same table.
bottlenecks.symptom: Advertiser queries immediately after 06:00 UTC batch completion run 5-20x slower (FINAL forces per-query merge); ClickHouse `system.merges` shows long-running merges saturating `background_pool_size`; `system.parts` row count for the T-1 partition stays elevated for hours; CPU on shards pins at 100% on merge threads, starving concurrent advertiser queries; occasional `Too many parts` errors block the streaming sink.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Run `OPTIMIZE TABLE ad_agg_1m PARTITION 'YYYYMMDD' FINAL` explicitly at end of batch job, off-peak, shard-by-shard with throttling; raise `background_pool_size` to 32+ and `max_bytes_to_merge_at_max_space_in_pool` to accommodate partition size; use `SELECT... FINAL` only in Report API and rely on the `argMax(source)` pattern against a materialized view pre-deduped per partition; consider switching to `AggregatingMergeTree` with explicit `insert` of tombstones instead of replace-on-merge for deterministic dedup.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `system.parts` active count per partition > 200; alert on `system.merges` queue depth > 20 sustained >5 min; track query p95 latency broken down by `FINAL` usage and alert on >2x regression post-batch; monitor `background_pool_size` utilization > 80%.

bottlenecks.title: Streaming sink part explosion from 1-minute window flushes across sharded fanout
bottlenecks.trigger: Flink emits per-(ad_id, minute) rows every minute — ~170K rows/min across ~10M active ads (bursty distribution). With sharding by `cityHash64(campaign_id)` across, say, 8 shards and 3x replication, each minute produces 8+ parts per shard (one per Flink subtask commit). Over 1 hour that's 480+ parts per partition per shard; ClickHouse's default `parts_to_throw_insert=300` is breached within 40 minutes if merges can't keep up.
bottlenecks.symptom: `DB::Exception: Too many parts (300). Merges are processing significantly slower than inserts` errors from the Flink sink; 2PC commits fail and Flink job restarts; checkpoint duration exceeds 30s interval; advertiser dashboards show stale data as the 1-min SLA slips to 5+ min; merge threads at 100% but can't catch up.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Batch Flink sink commits across multiple windows — emit one part per 30s checkpoint per shard (not per window), yielding ~2 parts/min/shard instead of 8+; raise `parts_to_throw_insert` to 600 and `parts_to_delay_insert` to 300; pre-shard in Flink so each subtask writes to exactly one ClickHouse shard (no fanout); tune `merge_with_ttl_timeout=3600` and grow `background_pool_size` to 32; use native TCP protocol client not JDBC for 3-5x insert throughput.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `system.parts` active count per partition > 200 (warn) / > 280 (page); track ClickHouse `InsertQuery` errors with `Too many parts` substring; alert on Flink `Sink.numRecordsOutPerSecond` dropping while upstream input holds; dashboard parts-created-per-min vs. parts-merged-per-min per shard.

bottlenecks.title: Hot shard skew from cityHash64(campaign_id) with power-law advertiser distribution
bottlenecks.trigger: Sharding by `cityHash64(campaign_id)` distributes by campaign, but ad spend follows a power law — the top 100 advertisers drive 50%+ of the 1B clicks/day and 100B impressions/day. A single large campaign landing on one shard can deliver 5-10x the average shard load for both writes (170K rows/min disproportionately concentrated) and reads (advertiser dashboard queries at ~50 QPS aggregated, but concentrated on top campaigns' shards).
bottlenecks.symptom: One or two shards show 80%+ CPU while peers sit at 20%; query p99 for top-advertiser dashboards 3-5x worse than median; the hot shard's merge backlog grows faster than peers post-batch; replica lag on the hot shard exceeds the 3x replication's ability to keep ISR in sync; a shard failure disproportionately impacts revenue-critical advertisers.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Switch sharding key to `cityHash64(campaign_id, toYYYYMMDD(bucket_ts))` so each campaign's data spreads across all shards over time, trading slightly more cross-shard query fanout for even load; or maintain a manual shard-weight table that pins top-N campaigns to dedicated shards with more CPU/IO; use ClickHouse's `Distributed` table with `internal_replication=true` and add a read-replica tier for top campaigns; pre-aggregate to hourly/daily rollups in a materialized view so top-campaign reads hit smaller tables.
bottlenecks.detection: Dashboard per-shard `QueryProfile` CPU and `InsertedRows` and alert when max/median ratio > 3x; track per-campaign query latency p95 and alert when top-10 campaigns regress >2x; monitor per-shard `system.replication_queue` depth and alert on >1000 entries.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why ClickHouse is here For an ad click aggregation service, the whole point is that **advertisers log in and ask analytical questions**: "show me clicks and CTR for campaign X over the last 7 days, grouped by creative." That's a `GROUP BY` across millions of rows returning in under a second, run by hundreds of advertisers simultaneously. A transactional database like Postgres is built for "fetch this one row by id" — it would choke on scan-heavy aggregations over billions of rows. ClickHouse is columnar: it only reads the columns the query touches (say, `clicks` and `bucket_ts`), compresses them heavily, and is purpose-built for the slice-and-dice queries advertiser dashboards issue. ## What happens without it If you pointed the Report API at the raw S3 Parquet lake, a single "7-day campaign timeseries" query would scan tens of GB and take **minutes**, not seconds. Advertiser dashboards would time out on every page load, the Report API would fall over under ~50 concurrent queries, and Flink would have no downstream place to commit aggregates — the "streaming aggregates visible within 1 min" SLA becomes impossible. ## The number that forces it Flink produces roughly **14.4B aggregate cells/day** (10M active ads × 1440 minutes). Over a 5-day hot retention window that's ~72B rows. ClickHouse's `PARTITION BY toYYYYMMDD(bucket_ts)` with `ORDER BY (campaign_id, ad_id, bucket_ts)` means a 7-day campaign query touches only 7 daily partitions, skips to the campaign's sorted range within each, and scans maybe a few million compressed rows — seconds-range latency at 50 QPS. ## Trade-off You accept running a second datastore (on top of Kafka and S3) to get the query latency advertisers expect.

dlq.name: Dead Letter Queue
dlq.summary: Holds events too late for the streaming window or rejected by schema validation.

sections.heading: What lands here
sections.body:
- Clicks with `ts_server_ms` older than the current watermark by more than 2 min
- Schema violations (unknown ad_id at ingest time → stale cache; allowed to flow to DLQ and reconciled later)
- Events with duplicate event_id that arrived > 24h after the original

sections.heading: Retention
sections.body: 30 days. Inspected by on-call when DLQ QPS rises — a spike usually indicates a misbehaving SDK rollout or a clock-skewed region.

sections.heading: Reconciliation
sections.body: Batch corrector reads the DLQ along with the raw event lake so no revenue data is truly lost.

bottlenecks.title: DLQ volume spike from SDK/clock-skew incidents overwhelms 30-day retention
bottlenecks.trigger: A bad SDK rollout or regional NTP outage pushes >2% of events past the 2-min watermark. At 1B clicks/day + 100B impressions/day, even 1% late events = 10M clicks + 1B impressions/day = ~400GB/day of DLQ writes. With 30-day retention that balloons to 12TB+ of DLQ storage and saturates the batch corrector's input for days after the incident clears.
bottlenecks.symptom: DLQ topic disk usage climbs linearly; batch corrector job runtime grows from ~4h to 8h+ as it unions a massive DLQ partition with the raw lake; on-call paged for 'DLQ storage > 80%'; advertiser numbers swing wildly between T-1 batch run and T-2 batch run as late events from the incident day get reconciled.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Split DLQ into two tiers by severity: `dlq_schema` (small, 30-day retention) for schema violations and `dlq_late` (large, 7-day retention) for late-but-valid events since batch reconciles T-1 within 24h anyway. Sink `dlq_late` directly to S3 via Kafka Connect (same as raw lake) instead of keeping it on Kafka brokers. Cap per-topic DLQ write rate with a circuit breaker at Flink's side-output so a runaway skew incident doesn't self-DoS.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on DLQ topic `BytesInPerSec` > 3x 7-day baseline for >5 min; alert on DLQ broker disk usage > 60%; dashboard DLQ-to-main-topic ratio per hour and alert when ratio exceeds 2%.

bottlenecks.title: DLQ becomes a silent data-loss sink if batch corrector doesn't drain it
bottlenecks.trigger: The DLQ design assumes batch corrector reads DLQ alongside the raw lake. If the batch job silently skips the DLQ path (missing S3 prefix, schema mismatch on evolved DLQ records, IAM misconfig), events sitting in DLQ for up to 30 days are never aggregated. At 1% late-event rate that's 10M clicks/day × 30 days = 300M clicks of unbilled revenue before Kafka retention deletes them.
bottlenecks.symptom: Advertisers in skewed-clock regions consistently see lower totals even after batch reconciliation; no error is raised because the batch job 'succeeds'; discrepancy only surfaces when finance reconciles against publisher-side impression logs weeks later.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Add a batch-job assertion step: count DLQ records read per day vs DLQ records produced per day (from Kafka metrics); fail the job if >0.1% gap. Emit a per-event-type counter from Flink's side-output and require batch to account for every counter. Run a weekly shadow job that replays DLQ from S3 mirror into a diff table and alerts on non-zero diff vs main `ad_agg_1m`.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `dlq_records_consumed_by_batch / dlq_records_produced_by_flink < 0.999` for any given day; alert when DLQ topic's consumer-group lag for `batch-corrector` exceeds 1h at job runtime; weekly reconciliation-diff dashboard per campaign.

bottlenecks.title: Schema drift in DLQ records breaks batch-corrector reads
bottlenecks.trigger: DLQ holds events from all historical SDK versions that were rejected (unknown ad_id, schema violations). Over 30-day retention a new field added to the beacon (say, `dispatch_method` added for sendBeacon loss tracking) produces DLQ records with mixed schemas. Spark batch job's `spark.read.parquet` with schema-on-read can silently null-fill or throw `AnalysisException` depending on evolution direction.
bottlenecks.symptom: Batch corrector fails with 'cannot resolve column dispatch_method' or silently drops fields after an SDK release; on-call discovers the failure only when the 06:00 UTC SLA is missed; rerunning the job requires a one-off schema merge script.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enforce Avro schema registry on the DLQ topic same as main topics — reject writes that don't register a compatible schema. In the batch job use `mergeSchema=true` on Parquet reads and treat DLQ schema as the union of all registered versions. Add a schema-evolution CI check that replays a sample of DLQ records against the batch job before any SDK or Flink schema change ships.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on Schema Registry `compatibility_check_failed` events on the DLQ subject; alert on batch-job Spark stage failures containing `AnalysisException` or `cannot resolve`; monitor distinct schema-fingerprint count per DLQ partition and alert on >3 active versions simultaneously.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the DLQ is here For an ad click aggregation service, Flink's streaming aggregator makes a hard trade-off: it waits at most **2 minutes** past real time for late events before closing a window and emitting counts. That 2-minute watermark is what keeps the "<1 min SLA" promise to advertisers. But at 1B clicks/day + 100B impressions/day, even a tiny fraction of events arrive late — a phone was in a tunnel, a mobile carrier buffered beacons, or a regional edge POP caught up on a spill backlog after its Kafka link recovered. These late events are still real, billable clicks. The DLQ is where they land instead of being silently dropped, so the nightly batch corrector can reconcile them into the authoritative numbers. ## What happens without it If Flink just discarded late events, those clicks would vanish from the streaming path *and* never make it into batch (the batch corrector only knows about S3 + DLQ). An advertiser whose users are on flaky mobile networks would consistently be under-billed; the operator would see streaming and batch numbers roughly agree on a dashboard but both would be missing the same 0.5–2% of clicks with no trace. Debugging would be near-impossible because the dropped events leave no artifact. ## One concrete number At 11.6K clicks/sec sustained, a 1% late-event rate is **~10M clicks/day** hitting the DLQ — directly billable revenue that would otherwise disappear. Over a 30-day retention window that's 300M clicks preserved for reconciliation. ## Trade-off You accept running an extra topic (and the risk of it silently filling up) to guarantee no valid click is ever permanently lost.

s3.name: Raw Event Lake (S3)
s3.summary: Immutable Parquet files of every raw event, partitioned by date and hour for the batch corrector.

sections.heading: Layout
sections.body: `s3://ad-events/date=2026-04-24/hour=14/part-00042.parquet`. Kafka Connect sinks from the `ad_clicks` and `ad_impressions` topics, rolling files every 5 min or 256 MB.

sections.heading: Schema evolution
sections.body: Parquet + Avro schema registry handles added fields; batch corrector reads with schema-on-read.

sections.heading: Why not query S3 for dashboards
sections.body: Advertiser dashboards need seconds-range latency; raw Parquet scans take minutes. S3 is the authoritative lake; ClickHouse is the serving layer.

lost: Must operate a NameNode / DataNode cluster

bottlenecks.title: S3 small-file explosion from 5-min Kafka Connect rolls across many partitions
bottlenecks.trigger: Kafka Connect S3 sink rolls on 5 min OR 256 MB, whichever first. The clicks topic has 200 partitions and impressions has 500 partitions. Clicks at 11.6K/sec × 400B = ~4.6 MB/sec total across 200 partitions = ~23 KB/sec/partition → 5-min roll produces ~7 MB files (far below 256 MB). That's 200 parts × 12 rolls/hour × 24h = 57,600 small click files/day, plus 500 × 288 = 144,000 impression files/day that *do* hit 256 MB each — combined ~200K objects/day, ~6M/month.
bottlenecks.symptom: Nightly Spark batch corrector spends 30-60% of runtime in S3 LIST + file-open overhead rather than actual compute; job misses the 06:00 UTC SLA on heavier days; S3 LIST throttling (5500 req/s per prefix) triggers 503s during job startup; S3 API costs dominate the storage line-item on the monthly bill.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Raise Connect `flush.size` and `rotate.interval.ms` to target ~128 MB files for clicks (rotate every 30 min instead of 5 min since batch only runs nightly); run a compaction job post-ingest that rewrites small files into 256 MB Parquet using `OPTIMIZE`-style coalesce; use Hive-style partitioning `date=/hour=` with random prefix salt to avoid LIST hot-spotting; consider switching to Iceberg/Delta tables with auto-compaction and manifest-based file skipping instead of raw Parquet + path listing.
bottlenecks.detection: Dashboard S3 object count per `date=/hour=` prefix; alert when any hour has >500 objects on clicks or >800 on impressions. Monitor S3 `5xxErrorRate` and `ThrottledRequests` on the bucket; alert on >0. Track Spark batch job's `Input: Scheduler Delay` vs `Executor Run Time` ratio; alert when delay > 20% of runtime.

bottlenecks.title: Impression lake storage growth outpaces retention/cost planning
bottlenecks.trigger: Impressions at 1.16M/sec × 400B × 86400s = ~40 TB/day raw, ~8 TB/day Parquet+zstd at 5x compression. Annualized that's ~3 PB/year compressed for impressions alone. With 3x replication in S3 Standard and cross-region replication for DR, effective cost-bearing footprint doubles. Peak days (3x) produce ~24 TB/day compressed — a single Black Friday week adds ~170 TB.
bottlenecks.symptom: S3 storage line item grows by tens of thousands of dollars/month quarter over quarter; finance flags the lake as the #1 cost driver; attempts to run ad-hoc historical analyses over >90 days hit query costs in the thousands per job; GDPR/CCPA deletion requests become expensive full-lake rewrites.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Tier aggressively: S3 Standard for 7 days (batch corrector reach), S3 Standard-IA after 7 days, S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval after 30 days, Glacier Deep Archive after 90 days — configured via S3 Lifecycle rules. Drop impression-level raw retention to 90 days in hot tiers and keep only daily pre-aggregated impression rollups long-term. Enable S3 Intelligent-Tiering on the `date=/hour=` prefixes. Partition by `advertiser_id_bucket` too so GDPR deletions can drop whole prefixes.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on bucket size growth rate > forecast (e.g., >10 TB/day compressed for impressions); monthly cost-per-TB dashboard broken down by storage class; alert if >70% of data sits in Standard tier after 14 days. Track lifecycle rule transition counts via CloudWatch and alert on stalled transitions.

bottlenecks.title: Eventual-consistency and late-landing files skew batch corrector coverage
bottlenecks.trigger: Kafka Connect S3 sink commits offsets only after file upload succeeds, but at 200+ partitions × 12 rolls/hour, transient S3 5xx or network blips cause some files to land minutes-to-hours after their data window. Batch job kicks off 02:00 UTC for the prior day — any file still buffered in Connect or retrying an upload at 02:00 gets excluded from that night's correction. At 1B clicks/day even 0.01% of delayed files = 100K clicks missing from the authoritative batch run.
bottlenecks.symptom: Batch-corrected numbers disagree with streaming totals by small but unexplained margins that don't match the DLQ accounting; running the same batch job 24h later produces different results for the same logical date; finance reconciliation against publisher logs flags gaps that can't be traced to DLQ or sendBeacon loss.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Have Connect emit a `_SUCCESS`-style completion manifest per `date=/hour=` prefix only after all partitions have committed offsets past the hour boundary; batch corrector waits for T-1's 23:59 hour manifest before starting. Delay batch start to 03:00 UTC with a 3-hour safety margin past midnight. Implement a T-2 reconciliation pass that diffs the previous night's batch output against a re-run and writes delta rows with `source='batch_v2'`. Use Iceberg snapshots so batch reads a point-in-time consistent view.
bottlenecks.detection: Emit per-hour file-count and row-count from Connect as metrics; alert when any hour's row-count deviates >0.5% from the corresponding Kafka topic's produced count. Track `_SUCCESS` manifest lag per hour partition and alert if any T-1 hour is missing at batch start time. Weekly shadow-rerun diff dashboard comparing batch-v1 vs batch-v2 totals per campaign.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Raw Event Lake is here For an ad click aggregation service, the streaming pipeline (Flink → ClickHouse) is *fast but approximate* — it commits to a 2-minute watermark and a 24h RocksDB dedupe window, which means it can't see full-day context needed for real bot filtering ("this IP clicked 80 times in 60 seconds across 12 ads — all bots"). The Raw Event Lake is the permanent, immutable record of **every event that ever hit the edge**, stored cheaply so the nightly batch corrector can re-aggregate the whole day with full context and produce authoritative numbers that overwrite the streaming guesses. ## What happens without it If there were no S3 lake, a Flink bug that under-counted for 20 minutes would be permanently baked into advertiser bills — Kafka retention is only 7 days for clicks and 2 days for impressions, and ClickHouse only holds aggregates, not raw events. The operator would have no way to re-run history, advertisers would dispute invoices the pipeline can't defend, and fraud teams would have nothing to audit when a publisher is suspected of click farming. ## One concrete number Impressions alone generate **40 TB/day raw** (1.16M/sec × 400 bytes × 86400s). That's far too much to keep in Kafka (it would cost a fortune on broker NVMe with 3× replication) but perfectly reasonable in S3 at a few cents per GB-month, with lifecycle rules tiering older partitions to Glacier. S3's role is exactly this: the only tier where ~15 PB/year of raw events is economically sane. ## Trade-off You accept minutes-long scan latency (S3 is useless for dashboards) in exchange for cheap, durable, replayable history.

batch.name: Batch Corrector
batch.summary: Nightly Spark job that re-aggregates the full day's raw events and overwrites streaming aggregates with 'batch' rows.

sections.heading: Why a separate batch job
sections.body: Bot filtering, late events, currency conversion, and fraud scoring all require cross-event context (e.g., 'more than 50 clicks in 60s from same IP hash = bot'). The stream can't see that without huge state. Batch can.

sections.heading: Job
sections.body:
```scala
spark.read.parquet(s"s3://ad-events/date=$d/").union(spark.read.parquet(s"s3://ad-dlq/date=$d/")).transform(applyBotFilter).transform(deduplicateByEventId).groupBy($"ad_id", $"campaign_id", window($"ts_server_ms", "1 minute")).agg(count("*").as("clicks"), approx_count_distinct($"user_id_hash").as("uniq_users")).withColumn("source", lit("batch")).write.jdbc(clickhouseUrl, "ad_agg_1m", SaveMode.Append)
```

sections.heading: SLA
sections.body: Job kicks off at 02:00 UTC for the prior day; must complete by 06:00 UTC so advertisers see corrected numbers when they log in.

sections.heading: What it corrects
sections.body:
- Late events that missed the 2-min watermark
- Bot clicks filtered with full-day context
- Streaming-path bugs (e.g., a bad deploy that under-counted for 20 min) — re-running batch fixes history without a replay of the streaming layer

gained: Simpler: one SQL job, no separate Spark cluster
lost: Less ergonomic bot-filtering logic than Spark/DataFrames

bottlenecks.title: Full-day dedupe shuffle on 1B+ events blows past executor memory/disk
bottlenecks.trigger: `dropDuplicates("event_id")` on the unioned events+DLQ dataset (~1.02B rows × ~400B ≈ 440 GB raw, ~80-100 GB Parquet-compressed) forces a full shuffle keyed by event_id across the 800-parallelism cluster. Peak days at 3x push this to ~3B rows / ~1.3 TB raw. Shuffle write amplification (spill + serialization) typically 2-3x the input.
bottlenecks.symptom: Executors OOM or spill 100s of GB to local NVMe; stage retries and `FetchFailedException` from lost shuffle blocks; job runtime climbs from ~4h to 8h+ and misses the 06:00 UTC SLA; ClickHouse batch rows not visible when advertisers log in at 08:00 local.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Replace global `dropDuplicates` with a bucketed pre-aggregation: `repartition(2000, $"event_id")` then per-partition dedupe so each task handles ~500K keys fitting in memory; enable AQE (`spark.sql.adaptive.enabled=true`, `spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled=true`); use `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions=2000` (up from default 200); enable `spark.shuffle.service.enabled=true` with external shuffle service so executor loss doesn't lose shuffle data; size executors with `spark.executor.memoryOverhead=4g` and NVMe-backed `spark.local.dir`.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on Spark stage duration > 2x 7-day baseline; monitor `ShuffleWriteBytes` and `DiskBytesSpilled` per stage, alert when spill > 50% of shuffle write; track job wall-clock and alert when projected finish > 05:30 UTC; dashboard executor OOM kill count per run.

bottlenecks.title: Bot-filter full-day windowing creates hot partitions on top IPs/campaigns
bottlenecks.trigger: `BotFilter.applyFullDay` computes '>50 clicks in 60s from same ip_trunc' which requires keying by `ip_trunc` (or `ip_trunc, ad_id`) and windowing across the full day. A /24 truncation collapses large NAT ranges — a single mobile carrier or corporate egress can concentrate 10-100M clicks/day on one key out of 1B total. At 800-task parallelism, one skewed key pins one task to single-threaded processing while 799 idle.
bottlenecks.symptom: Spark UI shows one straggler task running 30-60 min after peers complete; stage 'median task duration' is 2 min but 'max task duration' is 45 min; OOM on the straggler executor because the single key's windowed state exceeds memory; job SLA slips even when overall cluster is 10% utilized.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Salt the bot-filter key: `groupBy(concat($"ip_trunc", lit("_"), pmod(hash($"event_id"), lit(32))))` for a first-pass count, then re-aggregate across salts — spreads hot IPs 32-way; use Spark's AQE skew-join handling; or switch to a two-stage filter: pre-compute per-hour per-ip counts (even distribution) then flag IPs exceeding threshold, then re-scan and drop. Consider HyperLogLog-based approximate bot scoring so the join isn't needed.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on Spark `taskDurationMax / taskDurationMedian > 10x` for any stage; dashboard per-task input-rows histogram and alert when p99/p50 > 20x; track bot-filter stage wall-time and alert on >90 min (baseline ~15 min).

bottlenecks.title: JDBC write of 14.4M batch rows to ClickHouse serializes through a narrow connection pool
bottlenecks.trigger: The job writes ~14.4M aggregated rows/day (10M active ads × ~1.44 active minutes avg) via `write.jdbc(clickhouseUrl, "ad_agg_1m")`. Default Spark JDBC write uses 1 connection per partition but caps `numPartitions` typically at 8-32; at 14.4M rows through 16 JDBC connections = 900K rows/connection serialized, each connection running single-threaded INSERT. Followed by `OPTIMIZE... PARTITION FINAL` which rewrites the entire prior-day partition (~hundreds of GB across shards).
bottlenecks.symptom: Final write stage takes 30-90 min out of a 4h job; `OPTIMIZE... FINAL` runs another 30-60 min and pins ClickHouse merge threads at 100%, impacting streaming-sink inserts and advertiser query latency; occasional JDBC timeouts on large batches trigger stage retry that double-inserts rows (relying on ReplacingMergeTree to clean up later).
bottlenecks.mitigation: Switch to the ClickHouse native Spark connector (`com.clickhouse:clickhouse-spark-runtime`) using native TCP protocol — 3-5x faster than JDBC; shard-aware write that targets each ClickHouse shard directly from matching Spark partitions (no `Distributed` table fanout); run `OPTIMIZE PARTITION FINAL` shard-by-shard with throttling and off-peak to avoid starving streaming merges; set `spark.clickhouse.write.batchSize=100000` and parallelism matching shard count × 4.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on Spark write stage duration > 45 min; monitor ClickHouse `system.merges` queue depth during/after batch, alert on >20 sustained; track advertiser Report API p95 latency during 05:00-07:00 UTC window, alert on >2x regression; monitor JDBC connection pool wait time and retry count per batch run.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Batch Corrector is here For an ad click aggregation service at 1B clicks/day, the streaming path (Flink → ClickHouse) deliberately cuts corners to hit the "<1 min freshness" SLA: it only waits 2 minutes for late events, only dedupes event_ids for 24 hours, and can't do real bot filtering because that needs full-day context ("this IP hash clicked 80 times across 12 ads in 60 seconds — all bots"). Those corners mean streaming numbers are *approximate* — good enough for advertisers to watch a campaign trend live, but not good enough to bill against. The Batch Corrector is the nightly job that re-reads the full day's raw events from S3, applies proper bot filtering and dedupe, and overwrites the streaming aggregates with authoritative numbers. ## What happens without it Without the corrector, advertisers get billed on streaming numbers that include bot clicks (inflating their invoices and triggering disputes) and miss late events that arrived after the 2-min watermark (under-counting legitimate clicks). A streaming bug that under-counted for 20 minutes would be permanently baked into history — Kafka retention is only 7 days, so there'd be no way to replay and fix it. The fraud team would also have nothing to audit when a publisher is suspected of click farming. ## One concrete number The job processes ~1B events (~440 GB) each night and reduces them to ~14.4M aggregate rows (10M active ads × ~1.44 active minutes avg) — a ~70× reduction — and must finish in the 4-hour window between 02:00 and 06:00 UTC so advertisers see corrected numbers at login. ## Trade-off You accept maintaining two codebases (stream and batch) that must produce the same schema, in exchange for both low latency *and* eventual correctness.

reportapi.name: Report API
reportapi.summary: Thin read API in front of ClickHouse for advertiser dashboards and billing.

sections.heading: Endpoints
sections.body: `GET /campaign/{id}/timeseries?from=...&to=...&granularity=day` → clicks, impressions, CTR, uniq_users.

sections.heading: Query translation
sections.body: Builds parameterized ClickHouse SQL; uses `argMax(source)` to prefer batch rows over stream rows where both exist.

sections.heading: Caching
sections.body: Query results for completed days (T-1 and older) are cached in Redis for 24h — they can't change once batch has committed them.

sections.heading: Auth
sections.body: Per-advertiser OAuth token; queries force `WHERE advertiser_id =?` to the authenticated account — multi-tenant isolation at the query layer.

bottlenecks.title: FINAL / argMax(source) query cost on today's partition dominates latency
bottlenecks.trigger: Advertiser dashboards load 3 queries per page (summary, timeseries, per-creative) at ~50 QPS aggregate across 500 concurrent sessions. Today's partition in ClickHouse holds only `source='stream'` rows until batch runs, but the Report API uses `argMax(source)` or `FINAL` to prefer batch over stream where both exist. Once batch writes T-1 rows, FINAL forces per-query merge work across hundreds of unmerged parts (streaming sink flushes per-minute, producing ~170K rows/min split across shards). A 7-day timeseries query spans 1 batch-corrected day under reconciliation + 6 already-merged days + today (stream-only) — the middle day dominates CPU.
bottlenecks.symptom: Page load p95 jumps from <2s to 8-15s between 06:00-08:00 UTC right after batch completes; Report API thread pool saturates; advertisers on the east coast logging in at 08:00 local hit the worst window; ClickHouse `query_duration_ms` p99 spikes 5-10x; Redis hit rate for T-1 drops to zero after invalidation causing thundering herd on ClickHouse.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Split the query pattern: for T-2 and older (fully merged + cached) use a simple `SELECT... WHERE source='batch'`; for T-1 and today use `argMax(source)` against a narrower time range only. Run `OPTIMIZE TABLE ad_agg_1m PARTITION 'YYYYMMDD' FINAL` at end of batch before cache invalidation so queries never pay merge cost. Add a materialized view `ad_agg_1m_daily_final` pre-aggregated to day granularity for the common timeseries queries. Stagger Redis cache invalidation with jitter (5-10 min) and use `SETEX` with stale-while-revalidate to prevent herd.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on Report API p95 > 3s for >2 min; dashboard ClickHouse `query_duration_ms` broken down by `has_FINAL=true/false`; alert on Redis cache miss rate for `report:*` keys > 30% outside expected invalidation windows; track thread pool queue depth and alert at >50% capacity.

bottlenecks.title: Multi-tenant isolation failure via missing advertiser_id predicate
bottlenecks.trigger: Design forces `WHERE advertiser_id =?` at the query layer for isolation, but ClickHouse's `ORDER BY (campaign_id, ad_id, bucket_ts)` does not lead with `advertiser_id`. A bug or refactor that drops the predicate — or a campaign_id collision across advertisers after a data migration — exposes cross-tenant data. Also: queries that omit the predicate still execute (ClickHouse has no row-level security by default) and scan all shards returning other advertisers' numbers. At 500 concurrent sessions × 2 queries/load this is a blast radius of thousands of responses before detection.
bottlenecks.symptom: Advertiser sees campaign IDs they don't own in API responses; support ticket escalates to a data-breach incident; audit logs show queries without advertiser_id predicate succeeded; post-mortem reveals a code path (e.g., admin/internal tool sharing the same API) that bypassed the auth middleware.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enforce the predicate at two layers: (1) a query-builder that refuses to emit SQL without `advertiser_id =:auth_advertiser_id` — not a string template, a typed AST; (2) ClickHouse row policies (`CREATE ROW POLICY`) keyed on a session variable set from the OAuth token, so even a malformed query can't leak. Add `advertiser_id` as the leading column in a dedicated projection or secondary ORDER BY so the predicate is also a performance guard (queries without it become slow and alert). Integration test that every endpoint rejects requests with mismatched token vs. query param.
bottlenecks.detection: Log every ClickHouse query with `auth_advertiser_id` and extracted-from-SQL `predicate_advertiser_id`; alert immediately when they differ or when predicate is absent. Audit dashboard of top-10 queries by rows-scanned; any query scanning >10x the median for a single-advertiser request is suspicious. Weekly pen-test that tries cross-tenant access via manipulated campaign_id.

bottlenecks.title: Redis cache stampede on T-1 invalidation after batch completion
bottlenecks.trigger: Batch corrector completes around 05:30-06:00 UTC and the Report API invalidates all `report:*:2026-04-23*` keys in a single `redis.del` sweep. At 08:00-10:00 UTC local across major markets, ~500 concurrent advertisers load dashboards; each page issues 3 queries for T-1 data that was just invalidated — ~1500 simultaneous cache misses funneling to ClickHouse. Combined with the FINAL cost (bottleneck #1) and the 50 QPS steady-state, effective peak on ClickHouse is 10-20x normal for 5-10 min.
bottlenecks.symptom: ClickHouse query queue depth spikes right after cache invalidation; Report API p99 latency jumps to 10-30s; some requests time out and clients retry, amplifying load; ClickHouse CPU pegged at 100% across all shards for several minutes; advertiser Slack complaints about slow dashboards correlate with daily batch completion time.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Replace bulk `DEL` with lazy invalidation: set a `version:2026-04-23` key incremented on batch completion; cache keys include the version, so old keys just expire via TTL without a herd. Use `SET NX` single-flight (only one request per key repopulates, others wait on a short-lived lock with 2s timeout). Pre-warm cache as the last step of the batch job by running the top-N advertisers' common queries before opening the cache for reads. Add per-query jittered TTL (24h ± 15 min) so natural expiry doesn't cluster.
bottlenecks.detection: Dashboard Redis `keyspace_misses` rate and alert on >5x baseline sustained >1 min; track ClickHouse concurrent query count and alert at >2x 7-day p95; monitor Report API p99 latency vs. batch-completion timestamp and alert when post-batch p99 regression exceeds 3x for >3 min.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Report API sits in front of ClickHouse For an ad click aggregation service, the whole pipeline exists so advertisers can log in and see "how is my campaign doing?" — but you can't let their browsers talk directly to ClickHouse. Three things have to happen on every request that ClickHouse itself won't do: **authentication** (which advertiser is asking?), **tenant isolation** (force `WHERE advertiser_id =?` so Advertiser A can't see Advertiser B's numbers), and **reconciling the dual-source rows** (streaming wrote `source='stream'`, batch later wrote `source='batch'` for the same minute — the API uses `argMax(source)` to always return the best-available number). The Report API is the thin layer that owns those three concerns. ## What happens without it If dashboards hit ClickHouse directly, a malformed or malicious query could scan every advertiser's data, leak cross-tenant rows, or run a 30-second `GROUP BY` that starves the shard and blocks everyone else's dashboard. You'd also have no place to cache — every page load would re-scan billions of rows for data that, for yesterday and earlier, cannot possibly change. ## One concrete number The capacity plan expects **~500 concurrent advertisers × 2 queries per load ≈ 50 QPS** on OLAP, with each page firing 3 parallel queries (summary, timeseries, per-creative). That's ~1500 in-flight queries at peak. Caching completed days (T-1 and older) in Redis for 24h — since batch-committed rows are immutable — drops the real ClickHouse load by roughly the ratio of historical-to-today queries, typically 5–10×. ## Trade-off You accept an extra network hop and a caching layer to keep queries fast, secure, and multi-tenant-safe.

dashboard.name: Advertiser Dashboard
dashboard.summary: Web UI where advertisers see campaign performance.

sections.heading: Behaviour
sections.body: Loads summary numbers, then a per-day time series, then per-creative breakdown — 3 queries per page load, served in parallel from the Report API.

sections.heading: Latency expectation
sections.body: < 2s for a full page. A small 'Data may update until T+24h' note explains why today's numbers can move.

bottlenecks.title: 3-queries-per-page fan-out amplifies Report API load at login peaks
bottlenecks.trigger: Each page load issues 3 parallel queries (summary, timeseries, per-creative). With ~500 concurrent advertisers logging in at regional morning peaks (e.g., 08:00-10:00 local), page-load bursts produce ~1500 in-flight queries against Report API in seconds — well above the 50 QPS steady-state baseline in the capacity plan. Compounds with Redis cache invalidation at 06:00 UTC when T-1 keys are dropped.
bottlenecks.symptom: Dashboard feels sluggish or partially loads — summary tile appears but timeseries/creative panels spin for 5-15s; users refresh, doubling load; p95 page load exceeds the <2s SLA; browser devtools show 3 concurrent `/campaign/{id}/*` requests all hitting the slow path simultaneously.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Collapse the 3 endpoints into a single batched `/campaign/{id}/overview` call server-side so Report API can share a single ClickHouse scan across summary+timeseries+creative using CTEs or `WITH` clauses; add client-side request coalescing (React Query / SWR with `staleTime`); stagger sub-panel loads (render summary first, defer creative breakdown below-the-fold until scroll).
bottlenecks.detection: Track ratio of Report API QPS to active-session count; alert when ratio > 4 (expected 3 + small margin). RUM metric for `time-to-all-panels-rendered` p95 > 2s sustained 5 min. Browser `Performance.getEntriesByType('resource')` histogram of parallel-request count per page load.

bottlenecks.title: 'Numbers jumped overnight' user-trust breakage from stream→batch swap
bottlenecks.trigger: Streaming aggregates are approximate (2-min watermark, 24h dedupe, no full-context bot filtering) and batch reconciliation at 06:00 UTC can move T-1 numbers by 1-5% — larger for advertisers in bot-heavy or mobile-skewed traffic. An advertiser viewing a $50K campaign at 23:00 local sees one CTR, logs in next morning and sees a materially different number. With 500 concurrent advertisers this generates persistent support load.
bottlenecks.symptom: Support tickets citing 'clicks disappeared overnight' or 'why did CTR drop without me changing anything'; advertisers screenshot pre- and post-batch dashboards for disputes; trust in real-time numbers erodes and users stop checking intraday; finance team fields billing questions even though batch numbers are correct.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Render per-row `source` badge (`● Live` vs `✓ Final`) with tooltip explaining the 24h reconciliation window; gray out today+T-1 numbers with a subtle 'preliminary' style until batch-corrected; show a delta summary on login ('Yesterday's final numbers: -2.1% vs preliminary') so the change is explained not hidden; expose the 'Data may update until T+24h' note prominently near the numbers, not buried in a footer.
bottlenecks.detection: Instrument dashboard for 'stream vs batch delta' per campaign on T-1 transition; alert product team when median absolute delta > 3% (indicates bot-filter or dedupe drift worth investigating). Track support ticket tags for `number-changed` and alert on spike > 2x 7-day baseline.

bottlenecks.title: Timeseries rendering chokes on fine-granularity long date ranges
bottlenecks.trigger: Advertisers selecting 'last 7 days, 1-minute granularity' request 7 × 1440 = 10,080 data points per metric × 3-5 metrics (clicks, impressions, CTR, uniq_users, spend) = 30k-50k points. Browser chart libraries (Chart.js, Recharts) lag or freeze the main thread rendering that many points; Report API also returns a multi-MB JSON payload over mobile connections.
bottlenecks.symptom: Dashboard tab becomes unresponsive for 3-10s after date-range change; 'page unresponsive' dialog on lower-end laptops; mobile Safari runs out of memory and reloads; network panel shows 5-10 MB JSON responses; users complain that zooming/panning the chart is janky.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Auto-select granularity based on range (1-min only for <24h, 1-hour for 1-7d, 1-day for >7d) — matches how advertisers actually read the data and aligns with ClickHouse's daily rollup materialized views; server-side downsample to max ~500 visible points using LTTB algorithm; use canvas-based charts (uPlot, Apache ECharts) instead of SVG for >1k points; stream responses with HTTP compression (`Content-Encoding: br`).
bottlenecks.detection: RUM `long-task` count > 3 per page load alerts on main-thread blocking; Report API response-size histogram, alert on p95 > 1 MB; client-side chart render-time metric, alert p95 > 500ms. Track granularity × range combinations per request and dashboard the top-10 heaviest queries.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Advertiser Dashboard exists in this design For an ad click aggregation service, the entire pipeline — edge ingest, Kafka, Flink, ClickHouse, nightly batch corrector — exists for exactly one human-visible reason: **advertisers need to see how their campaigns are performing**. Without a dashboard, you've built a beautifully engineered data pipeline that produces numbers no one can look at. It's the consumption surface that justifies the 1B clicks/day of infrastructure behind it. It's also where the *dual-path* nature of the system (fast stream + authoritative batch) becomes user-visible: the dashboard has to explain to a human why the number they saw at 11pm moved 2% by morning. ## What happens without it If advertisers had to query ClickHouse directly or read raw S3 Parquet, they'd need to write SQL, understand `argMax(source)` to reconcile stream vs batch rows, and know which partitions exist. Instead, they'd churn — and your sales team would lose accounts to competitors who ship a UI. The Report API would also have no well-defined consumer shaping its endpoints, so query patterns would sprawl and caching would be impossible to tune. ## One concrete number The capacity plan assumes **~500 concurrent advertisers × 2 queries per page load = ~50 QPS on OLAP**. But each page actually fires 3 parallel queries (summary, timeseries, per-creative), so in login-peak bursts that's ~1500 in-flight queries hitting Report API within seconds — which is exactly why Redis caches T-1 and older days (immutable once batch commits) to absorb the fanout. ## Trade-off You accept building and maintaining a UI (plus explaining the "numbers may update until T+24h" quirk) in exchange for a product advertisers will actually pay for.

operations.title: Ingest a click event
operations.name: Ingest a click event
operations.description: A user clicks an ad; the SDK beacons the edge; the edge stamps and publishes to Kafka; raw event is mirrored to S3 by Kafka Connect.

steps.title: SDK fires click beacon
steps.action: On click, the SDK builds a JSON event with a fresh UUID and uses `navigator.sendBeacon` so the page can navigate to the advertiser landing URL without waiting.

steps.title: Edge stamps and validates
steps.action: The nearest edge POP accepts the beacon, stamps `ts_server_ms`, truncates the IP for privacy, validates schema, and produces to Kafka. Returns 204 immediately.

steps.title: Kafka appends click to partition log
steps.action: Broker appends the record to the partition determined by `hash(ad_id) % 200`. acks=all; returns once ISR has 2 replicas fsynced.

steps.title: Kafka Connect sinks raw event to S3 (parallel)
steps.action: A separate Kafka Connect S3 sink task subscribes to `ad_clicks` and writes Parquet files rolled every 5 min or 256 MB. This runs in parallel with the streaming aggregator — it feeds the nightly batch corrector.
steps.note: This is fire-and-forget from the ingest path's perspective — the event is already durable in Kafka.

operations.title: Stream-time aggregation (1-minute tumbling window flush)
